fields.story: I learned to weave from my mother when I was eight years old, sitting beside her on the veranda in Atori. She showed me how to split the pandanus leaf just right — too thick and the weave looks rough, too thin and it tears. Every bag I make carries that patience she taught me.
fields.portrait_alt: Portrait of Julie Mone from Atori, Guadalcanal Province

fields.story: I carve because my father carved, and his father before him. In Munda we have always worked with kerosene wood — it is hard and beautiful when you finish it smooth. I make bowls and trays that people use every day. I like that something I shape with my hands ends up on someone's table far away.
fields.portrait_alt: Portrait of Peter Kera from Munda, Western Province

fields.description: Traditionally in Melanesian culture, men learn to carve and women learn to weave. For some women, particularly those from Rennell and Bellona Province, weaving is a way of life and a part of their identity. Most bags and mats are made from the leaves of the pandanus tree.
fields.cultural_context: In many Solomon Islands communities, weaving knowledge is passed from mother to daughter. Specific patterns may belong to particular families or clans and carry stories of origin, place, and kinship.

fields.description: Hand-carved wooden bowls with pearl shell and/or wood inlay design are polished and sealed. The oval-shaped bowls are carved from kerosene wood (Cordia subcordata), which has a warm brown tone and is termite resistant.
fields.cultural_context: Carving traditions vary by island and province. In Western Province, nguzunguzu (ship prow figures) are carved as protective spirits for canoes.
